slides.title: Searching
slides.content:
# Search Algorithms 🔍

## Linear Search O(n)
Check one by one. Works on unsorted data.

## Binary Search O(log n)
Divide and conquer! **Requires sorted data**.
1. Check middle.
2. If target < mid, search left.
3. If target > mid, search right.
4. Repeat.

> 💡 **Fun Fact**: Binary search can find a specific atom in the observable universe in just ~270 steps!

slides.title: Basic Sorting
slides.content:
# Quadratic Sorts O(n²) 🐢

Good for teaching, bad for production.

## Bubble Sort
Repeatedly swap adjacent elements if they are in wrong order. Largest element "bubbles" to top.

## Selection Sort
Find minimum, swap to front. Repeat for rest.

## Insertion Sort
Take element, insert into correct position in sorted part. Very fast for **small** or **nearly sorted** arrays.

slides.title: Efficient Sorting
slides.content:
# Log-Linear Sorts O(n log n) 🐇

## Merge Sort
Divide array in half, sort halves recursively, then **merge** sorted sorted halves. 
- **Pros**: Stable, consistent O(n log n).
- **Cons**: Uses O(n) extra space.

## Quick Sort
Pick a "pivot", partition array (smaller left, larger right), recurse.
- **Pros**: Very fast in practice, in-place.
- **Cons**: Worst case O(n²) if bad pivot.

slides.title: Sorting Quiz
slides.quizQuestion: Which sorting algorithm is typically fastest in practice but has a bad worst-case?

slides.title: Python's Sort
slides.content:
# Timsort 🐍

Python's `sorted()` and `list.sort()` use **Timsort**.

- Hybrid of **Merge Sort** and **Insertion Sort**.
- Takes advantage of existing order in real-world data.
- **Best Case**: O(n)!
- **Average/Worst**: O(n log n).
- **Stable**: Preserves order of equal elements.
